To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the main prey of the lesser kestrel, Orthoptera, showed complex patterns of abundance in agricultural landscapes.

1) Orthoptera density was higher in semi-natural habitats and field margins, 2) Orthoptera density varied among crop types and localities, and 3) the abundance and distribution of Orthoptera was not solely explained by crop composition around lesser kestrels colonies.
Orthoptera abundance in arable fields surrounding lesser kestrel nests was highly variable and that semi-natural habitats were the main prey reservoirs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conservation of farmland Orthoptera as a food resource for lesser kestrels and other farmland bird species.
the conservation of lesser kestrels and Orthoptera, and the results can also be applied to other species and ecosystems.
the conservation of lesser kestrels in farmed landscapes, but also with other farmland species and the maintenance of biodiversity in agricultural landscapes in general.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the lesser kestrel is a species that is sensitive to changes in land management, and that it is not possible to generalize the effects of land use on prey abundance, and thus, lesser kestrel breeding success.
the lesser kestrel is not a good indicator of Orthoptera abundance, and therefore of the conservation value of farmed habitats.
a more diverse agricultural landscape is better for the lesser kestrel, but this is also true for many other farmland bird species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conservation of Orthoptera populations is a crucial issue to ensure the conservation of the lesser kestrel in arable landscapes, but it is not sufficient.
conservation of lesser kestrels should be based on a holistic approach to landscape management, including the conservation of semi-natural habitats and edge effects.
Orthoptera abundance is a key factor in lesser kestrel breeding success.
The main takeaway from our work is that
conservation of lesser kestrels and many other declining farmland bird species will be more successful if it is integrated with conservation measures for farmland biodiversity.

conservation of Orthoptera populations and lesser kestrels will require a holistic landscape approach that considers not only the conservation of the main prey species but also the conservation of the habitats that sustain them.

the conservation and restoration of semi-natural habitats in agricultural landscapes should be prioritized to enhance prey abundance and diversity and to increase the conservation value of such landscapes for lesser kestrels and other declining farmland bird species.
